newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Madelin wins party power base.
newsitem.headline: France's Madelin wins party power base.

text.p: French free-marketeer and former finance minister Alain Madelin was elected leader of the opposition Republican Party (PR) on Tuesday, giving him a power base if he can widen the divided group.

With his chances of a new government role in tatters after the left's upset election victory this month, Madelin hopes to turn the right-wing group into a broad liberal party to vie for power in the next election, by 2002.
"I know precisely how to bring together all of the branches of our family in order to create a strong movement," Madelin told party faithful after the vote.
"We are today the newest, most modern and most open group in French political life," he said.
But Pierre-Andre Wiltzer, a member of the centre-right umnbrella group, the Union for French Democracy (UDF), warned that only a united group could succeed in politics.
"The liberals and the Christian Democrats must join forces and their ideas and avoid the trap of rivalry," he said.

Madelin, 51, won 59.9 percent of the vote at a PR national congress in the Paris suburb of Levallois to 37.28 percent for deputy Gilles de Robien and 2.82 percent for former parliamentarian Philippe Mathot.
He immediately asked that the party's name be changed to Liberal Democracy, a proposal adopted on a show of hands.
De Robien, portraying himself as an alternative to Madelin's "ultra-liberal" views, had mounted a last-minute challenge in order, he said, to preserve democracy within the party.
He had announced his candidacy in a paid newspaper advertisement, accusing the party of withholding its mailing list from him until it was too late to write to members.
Ex-defence minister Francois Leotard had agreed to yield the presidency of the PR while remaining leader of the UDF.

The PR currently counts just 41 deputies in the National Assembly, compared to 106 prior to the June 1 parliamentary election which devastated the centre-right majority and swept a leftist union of Socialists, Communists and Greens into power.
The PR leadership nonetheless gave Madelin the power base he has lacked throughout his chequered career.
Three times a cabinet member, he was sacked as finance minister after only a few months in 1995 for attacking civil servants' privileges.
The PR congress was part of a series of moves to reorganise a French right badly shaken by its unexpected election fiasco.

The UDF's senior partner in opposition, the Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR) founded by President Jacques Chirac, will also change leaders at a July 6 congress after ex-prime minister Alain Juppe was forced to step down.

Socially-minded Gaullist Philippe Seguin is set to take over the party. Chirac had briefly anointed an unlikely duo of Seguin and Madelin as the right's standard bearers last month in a doomed last-minute bid to stave off electoral defeat after Juppe's withdrawal.

Madelin says he wants to unite all economic liberals now scattered among other parties, and win back disgruntled conservative voters who have deserted mainstream parties for the far-right, anti-immigrant National Front, which polled 15 percent in the recent parliamentary poll's first round.

Madelin faces a hard task rebuilding a party still reeling from a rift in the 1995 presidential election when most of its leaders backed the loser, Gaullist Edouard Balladur. Madelin supported Chirac.
The PR, the second largest group in the UDF with 33,000 members, is also beset by financial and legal problems.

Its coffers are reportedly almost empty and it is under investigation on suspicion of illicit funding involving cash deposits of millions of francs (dollars) channelled through offshore bank accounts and front companies in Panama, Luxembourg and Switzerland.
